transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-14
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE); Priya Patel (Redwood SE); Daniel Cho (Head of ML, Novus); Maya Rivera (Platform Eng, Novus); Ethan Brooks (CTO, Novus)

Summary (auto): Quick walkthrough of Optimize recommendations focusing on lookup TTLs, prefix cache hit-rate tradeoffs, and batching. Showed a cost-sim with sample numbers. Action items: send spreadsheet, stand up sandbox, share prompts.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. I think we have about 50 minutes, is that still good?
[00:06] Daniel (Novus): Yep that's perfect, thanks Alex. Quick context — we run a multi-tenant chat assistant, around 1.2k QPS peak distributed over the day, average session length like 220 tokens, and we are very sensitive to per-token costs.
[00:22] Priya (Redwood SE): Thanks for the context Daniel, that helps. Today we want to focus on lookup and TTL strategies for the prefix/KV cache plus batching knobs in the console and how that flows into the cost-sim. We'll call out where latency tradeoffs are made.
[00:36] Maya (Novus): Quick nit, when you say "lookup" you mean the K V lookups for session cache?
[00:40] Priya: Yeah, sorry, our speech to text — kay vee, K V, KV — all the same. It's the per-request prefix or session key lookup into the KV store we use to avoid re-sending prefixes each time.
[00:50] Ethan (Novus): And TTL is the time-to-live for those entries? Like how long the prefix stays hot in the cache?
[00:54] Alex: Exactly. We'll show a couple of approaches — longer TTLs, shorter TTLs, adaptive TTLs by customer, and also a sharded TTL strategy that reduces memory overhead.
[01:04] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[01:07] Priya: Sorry, there was a brief audio cut. Ok, jumping into the console — I'll share my screen.
[01:14] [screen share starts]
[01:18] Priya: On the left under Optimize -> Caching, here's our prefix cache config. You can see the global TTL default, per-model overrides, and a per-customer policy option.
[01:30] Daniel: Can you show the hit-rate estimator?
[01:33] Priya: Yep. This estimator takes your QPS, session length, and assumed reuse to project hit-rate for a given TTL. For example, with your numbers — 220 tokens avg, sessions with 3 requests in 2 minutes — a TTL of 5 minutes yields about 46% hit rate in our sim.
[01:48] Maya: That seems low; where's the rest of the win coming from?
[01:51] Priya: There are two levers: hit rate from prefix reuse and batching. If you increase batching you amortize model throughput cost across concurrent requests. For example, at 1.2k peak QPS with a batch window of 20ms you get continuous batching of small groups; bump that to 80ms you can get bigger batches but add additional latency.
[02:07] Alex: I'll pause — one question we always ask — what's your P95 latency SLO for user-facing calls?
[02:12] Daniel: We target <=250ms P95 for typing responses, but for longer generative replies we can tolerate up to 800ms.
[02:19] Alex: Great, that gives us headroom to tune batching in the 40-80ms window in some endpoints, while keeping interactive flows lower.
[02:26] [03:00] Priya: Now the cost sim — I'll switch to the spreadsheet view. We have three scenarios: conservative, baseline (your current), and aggressive. Each scenario toggles TTL, batch window, and quantization model choice.
[03:12] Maya: Walk me through the numbers for the baseline.
[03:16] Priya: Baseline assumes 5-minute TTL, 30ms batch window, and moderate batch efficiency; that gave us about 34% token savings vs cold (no cache) in the sim — total cost reduction of ~28% once you factor batching.
[03:31] Ethan: Wait 28% total — can you break down where that 34% token savings comes from?
[03:35] Priya: Sure — roughly 20 percentage points are from prefix reuse (so you don't re-send previous system/prompt tokens), ~10 points from KV warm hits that avoid recomputation, and ~4 points from batching efficiency. The remaining delta is model quantization or smaller model fallback on low-priority routes in the aggressive scenario.
[03:55] Daniel: How sensitive is that to TTL accuracy? If people have long sessions but infrequent reuse, we might see diminishing returns.
[04:02] Priya: Absolutely. The estimator will show a sensitivity curve. For example if your effective reuse per session drops by 30%, the savings go from 28% to about 12-14% total. That's where an adaptive TTL helps — we can set TTL to decay based on per-customer session heatmap.
[04:18] Alex: One pattern we've seen is short TTL for public/free tenants and longer TTL for high-value, high-reuse customers — gives you a lot of bang for the buck while limiting memory.
[04:27] Maya: Do you support per-shard TTLs? Like TTL per customer segment stored in different partitions?
[04:31] Priya: Yes, you can configure per-customer TTL and whether that customer gets a hot shard. In our dedicated flow we also support pinned KV shards to keep warm on specific worker pools.
[04:42] [05:10] Priya: Now latency — if a request hits the KV cache we still need a small lookup cost, which is typically 2–6 ms depending on the backing store (in-memory vs remote). If your KV is remote across a VPC peering link it may be higher; we recommend colocating or using our in-process cache for the hottest prefixes.
[05:28] Daniel: For security, we can't expose ephemeral keys outside our VPC. How do you manage K M S and key wrapping in the private flow?
[05:35] Alex: Good callout — our Private offering supports customer K M S integration and HSMs for key material. We also provide an audit trail and per-token encryption at rest. We'll share the SOC two and K M S docs as part of the security packet.
[05:47] Maya: Perfect. Also need RBAC for engineering vs support.
[05:51] Priya: Console supports role-based policies that can lock down TTL changes and model fallbacks.
[05:55] [06:40] Priya: Back to the costing, here's a scenario where we drop TTL to 60s but increase batch window to 80ms; you see a change — hit rate drops to ~28% but batching improvement recovers some of that loss; net savings ends up roughly similar but with lower memory footprint and slightly higher tail latency.
[07:01] Ethan: Tradeoff matrices like that are helpful. Could you show a recommended default for us if we want to prioritize cost but keep P95 < 350ms?
[07:09] Priya: For your stated SLOs I'd recommend 3-minute TTL for standard tenants, 10-minute TTL for VIP tenants, batch window 40ms for chat completions and 20ms for interactive microflows. That gives an estimated 30-40% cost reduction with P95 in your target.
[07:25] Daniel: That 10-minute VIP TTL — wouldn't that blow up memory for multi-tenant?
[07:30] Priya: It can; that's why we recommend hot-shard pinning only for a handful of customers and use probabilistic sampling to evict rarely used prefixes. Also we support compressed prefix storage and approximate LRU to keep memory bounded.
[07:43] [08:10] Priya: I want to show an adaptive TTL rule: TTL = base_ttl * (1 + reuse_score). The reuse_score is derived from session frequency and same-user reuse. So customers with many quick repeats get TTL extended automatically.
[08:25] Maya: How do you compute reuse_score without exposing PII?
[08:28] Priya: It's computed on hashed session IDs and aggregated metrics; we store only counters and heatmaps, not raw prompts, so it meets most privacy constraints. We'll include the technical note in the security packet.
[08:40] [09:00] Alex: Let's talk about measurement. For your sandbox run we'll do traffic replay for a 72-hour window to capture diurnal patterns. We'll instrument token-level cost, latencies, hit rates, and cache occupancy.
[09:12] Daniel: Replay — do you need us to provide raw logs or replay harness?
[09:16] Priya: Ideally a replayable trace (timestamps, prompt length, user/session id hash). If that's not possible we can take sampled logs and reconstruct QPS and token distributions. Maya said she'll check feasibility.
[09:26] Maya: Yep I'll try to extract a 48–72 hour trace and scrub it.
[09:30] [10:00] Priya: Ok, now one more advanced pattern — model routing fallback. If a prefix has low hit probability we can route to a smaller quantized model for first pass and only escalate to the larger model on fallback. That nets additional cost savings but adds complexity in correctness.
[10:18] Ethan: Do you have examples where that was safe?
[10:21] Priya: We ran a customer pilot where a two-tier model reduced average token cost by ~18% with negligible quality regression on short informational queries. For multi-turn, we prefer caching and warm paths to avoid fallback jitter.
[10:33] Daniel: What about eventual consistency — if a prefix is updated, how quickly does it reflect across the cluster?
[10:38] Priya: We keep boundaries configurable. By default, writes are propagated within 500ms-2s across hot nodes; you can require strong consistency on updates in private deployments but that will increase latency.
[10:50] [12:00] (cross talk, laughter)
[12:05] Alex: Quick pause for questions — are there any blockers from a procurement or security perspective?
[12:10] Ethan: Procurement timeline could be 4-6 weeks; we need a budget line item. We'll try to expedite if the sandbox runs show the expected savings.
[12:19] Alex: Understood — we'll write up a one-pager on expected ROI to help with procurement.
[12:24] Maya: Also need a short SOC two checklist for our security review board.
[12:28] Alex: We'll include that in the packet.
[12:32] [14:00] Priya: Back to the sim — I've toggled an aggressive scenario: TTL 15 minutes for VIPs, 60s for normal, batch window 60ms. That shows up to 52% token reduction in the model invocation cost line but with increased working set. You can see a chart where memory grows with TTL, and the sim shows cost vs infra tradeoff.
[14:20] Daniel: Can you export that chart as CSV?
[14:22] Priya: Yep, we'll send the full spreadsheet and CSV.
[14:26] Maya: One thing — our infra team prefers not to have managed memory spikes; can you set upper bounds on cache occupancy per shard?
[14:33] Priya: Absolutely. You can set max entries per shard and a percentile-based eviction so spikes won't cross a hard limit.
[14:39] [16:00] Alex: I'll sketch the recommended next steps: 1) we send cost sim + sample configs (Alex), 2) Redwood spins up sandbox with traffic replay (Priya), 3) Novus provides scrubbed trace and target prompt set (Maya), 4) run 72-hour benchmark and compare cost/latency (joint).
[16:20] Daniel: Sounds good. What about production rollout — how would we stage TTL changes?
[16:25] Priya: We have rollout controls: canary by tenant, percent ramp, and automatic rollback on latency or error regressions. We'll help you configure canary thresholds.
[16:36] Ethan: And monitoring for regressions — is there alerting integrated?
[16:40] Alex: Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency, and hit-rate dashboards. You can hook alerts to PagerDuty or Slack for any SLO breaches.
[16:48] [18:00] Daniel: If we see less savings than predicted, what's the usual root cause?
[18:04] Priya: Often it's mismatch of session semantics — e.g., if most sessions are single-turn or prompts change per request then prefix reuse is low. Another is cold-start due to churned users. We usually recommend measuring reuse_score and forcing longer TTL only where reuse is real.
[18:18] Maya: Any gotchas with traffic replay accuracy?
[18:21] Priya: Make sure timestamps and ordering are preserved; concurrency shape matters a lot for batching. If you compress time you'll artificially inflate batching efficiency.
[18:31] [20:00] Alex: Alright, quick recap and actions. We'll send the sim spreadsheet and a short ROI one-pager. Priya will own the sandbox spin-up. Maya will provide a scrubbed trace. Daniel/Ethan will check procurement.
[20:15] Ethan: Thanks all. If the sandbox shows 30%+ savings it's an easy yes from my side.
[20:20] Alex: Great — we'll follow up by Thursday with the materials.
[20:25] (end of meeting)
